g9-chemistry-uc2-t1.overview: Chemistry is a measuring science: a reaction is only as good as your balance, your cylinder and your digits. This lesson sets the SI units chemists live by, the derived quantities they calculate, and the significant-figure rules that keep claims honest.
objectives: Recall the seven SI base units and the three used most in chemistry
Convert within metric prefixes (k, d, c, m, μ, n)
Compute derived quantities (volume, density) with correct units
Apply significant-figure rules in readings and calculations
g9-chemistry-uc2-t1.simple: The SI system is the world's one measuring language: metre (m) length, kilogram (kg) mass, second (s) time, plus kelvin (K), mole (mol), ampere (A), candela (cd). Prefixes slice it: milli = 1/1000, centi = 1/100, kilo = 1000. Chemistry's favorites: volume (L, dm³, cm³), density = mass ÷ volume (g/cm³), temperature in K (°C + 273). Every measurement carries significant figures: all the digits you're sure of plus one estimated — 2.50 g ≠ 2.5 g in precision. Accuracy = hitting the true value; precision = repeating tightly.
g9-chemistry-uc2-t1.detailed:
Why units matter: a number without a unit is meaningless (a 'dose of 5' kills or cures depending on the unit), and mismatched units have crashed spacecraft (the 1999 Mars Climate Orbiter — one team used pound-seconds, the other newton-seconds). The SI system, agreed internationally, defines seven base units; chemistry leans on the metre, kilogram, second, kelvin and mole.

Metric prefixes are decimal steps: kilo (10³), deci (10⁻¹), centi (10⁻²), milli (10⁻³), micro (10⁻⁶), nano (10⁻⁹). Converting is moving the decimal point: 1 m = 100 cm = 1000 mm; 1 kg = 1000 g; 1 L = 1000 mL = 1 dm³; 1 mg = 0.001 g. Practice the ladder method: each step ×10 or ÷10 by its exponent gap.

Derived quantities combine base units: area = m², volume = m³ with the practical 1 mL = 1 cm³; solids displaced water measure irregular volumes. Density (g/cm³ or kg/m³) = mass ÷ volume — an identifying property of a substance: water 1.0, iron 7.9, gold 19.3 g/cm³; it also predicts floating (wood < water sinks nothing; oil floats). Temperature in kelvin: K = °C + 273 (0 K = absolute zero, molecular motion minimal) — used whenever formulas need proportional temperature.

Significant figures communicate precision honestly. Rules: all non-zeros count; zeros between non-zeros count (2005 = 4 sf); leading zeros NEVER count (0.0025 = 2 sf — they only place the decimal); trailing zeros count ONLY with a decimal point (2.50 = 3 sf, 250 = 2 sf ambiguous — scientific notation fixes it: 2.5×10² vs 2.50×10²). Reading instruments: record all certain marks + one estimated digit (a meniscus at 24.0 mL on a cylinder graduated in 1 mL). In calculations: multiplication/division → fewest sf of any input; addition/subtraction → fewest decimal places. Intermediate steps keep extra digits; round once at the end (avoiding rounding-error snowball). Exact numbers (definitions, counted objects) have infinite sf.

Accuracy vs precision: hitting the true value (accuracy) needs correct calibration; repeating tightly (precision) needs a steady technique. A dartboard picture is the classic: throws clustered far from the bull = precise but not accurate; scattered around the center = accurate on average, imprecise. Chemists chase both with calibration and replicates.

Tools in the lab: triple-beam/electronic balance (mass, g), graduated cylinder (volume, rough), burette/pipette (volume, precise), thermometer, stopwatch; scientific notation handles absurd sizes (atom diameter ≈ 1×10⁻¹⁰ m, Avogadro 6.02×10²³) keeping every huge/tiny number readable and its sf explicit.

formulas.name: Density
formulas.meaning: mass divided by volume; units g/cm³ or kg/m³
formulas.example: iron piece 158 g in 20 cm³ → 158 ÷ 20 = 7.9 g/cm³ ✓ iron

workedExamples.problem: Convert 0.75 L to mL and cm³.

workedExamples.answer: (a) 3 (leading zeros dead, trailing after decimal counts), (b) 4 (sandwich zeros count), (c) 1 (no decimal point — ambiguous, write 1×10³ or 1.000×10³), (d) 4 (only the mantissa's digits count)

workedExamples.problem: A rock of 52.0 g raises water from 25.0 to 33.0 mL. Density?
workedExamples.calculation: V = 33.0 − 25.0 = 8.0 cm³ (2 sf by subtraction rule); ρ = 52.0 ÷ 8.0 = 6.5
workedExamples.answer: 6.5 g/cm³ — limited to 2 sf by the volume difference

workedExamples.problem: Three students weigh a 25.00 g standard: A gets 24.9, 25.1, 25.0; B gets 24.5, 24.6, 24.5; C gets 25.02, 24.98, 25.00. Who's accurate? precise? both?
workedExamples.answer: A: accurate on average, moderate precision. B: precise but NOT accurate (systematic error — balance needs calibration). C: both — tight AND true

commonMistakes: Counting leading zeros as significant (0.0025 has 2, not 4)
Reporting a calculator's full output (0.7 g/cm³ typed as 0.70234) — false precision
Confusing mL and mg — one is volume, the other mass; never 'convert' them directly
Mixing °C into formulas needing K (gas volumes halve wrongly at 0°C)
Rounding each intermediate step (round once, at the end)
Saying precision and accuracy mean the same thing
applications: Pharmacy: a 10× dosing error from mg/g confusion is a classic unit fatality
Gold-smuggling & scrap markets: density separates real gold (19.3) from fool's brass (8.4)
Cooking & agriculture: graduated scoops, dilute sprays and fertilizer bags are ratio math
Lab work for national exams: meniscus reading and burette technique are practical syllabus items
Water quality: turbidity and chlorine dose calculations ride on mL and ppm conversions
g9-chemistry-uc2-t1.summary: SI gives chemistry one language: metre–kilogram–second–kelvin–mole with decimal prefixes; density (m÷V) and volume link mass to space. Significant figures (leading zeros never count, trailing only after a decimal) and rounding by the weakest input keep numbers honest. Accuracy = truth, precision = repeatability — lab work aims for both.

g9-chemistry-uc2-t2.overview: The scientific method is chemistry's referee: propose, test, measure, revise. This lesson walks the method end-to-end and installs the lab-safety habits that make experiments survivable.
objectives: Sequence the scientific method steps with a worked example
Design a fair test: variable, control, replicate
State lab rules: handling acids, heating, waste, PPE
Recognize hazard symbols and safe responses
Explain why repeatable results matter more than one lucky trial
g9-chemistry-uc2-t2.simple: The method: observe → question → hypothesize → experiment → analyze → conclude → share. A good experiment changes ONE thing (independent variable), measures the response (dependent), keeps everything else fixed (constants) with a control to compare against — and repeats (replicates) so luck can't masquerade as pattern. In the lab: goggles on, tie long hair, waft never sniff, add acid to water (never water to acid), know the flame-out plan (fire blanket, not running). A hypothesis can't be 'proven' — only supported or rejected by evidence.
g9-chemistry-uc2-t2.detailed:
Observation (quantitative measurements and qualitative notices) sparks a question. A hypothesis is a testable, specific prediction — 'if surface area increases, then dissolving speeds up because more solid touches the solvent.' It becomes an experiment: manipulate the independent variable, measure the dependent, freeze the rest (temperature, stirring, volume) and run a control (unchanged baseline) plus replicates (repeat trials to average out random error). Analyze (tables → graphs → trends), conclude (support or reject; back to hypothesis if rejected), and communicate so others can reproduce — reproducibility is what separates science from anecdote. A model that survives all this becomes theory; one anomaly of honest measurement can beat ten confident opinions.

Lab safety is the method's precondition. Core rules: PPE (goggles, apron, closed shoes, tied hair); no tasting, never sniff directly (gently waft); know exits, water, fire blanket and first-aid box before starting. Chemistry-specific: acids and bases are corrosive — dilute slowly, always add acid to water (water into concentrated acid boils locally and spits acid); when heating test tubes, point the mouth away from people, use a test-tube holder, never seal a heated vessel; mercury thermometers broken = report, never handle with bare hands; glassware chipped = discard bin, not sink; waste goes to labelled containers, not drains, per teacher instruction.

Hazard symbols (GHS pictograms): flammable (flame), corrosive (drips eating metal/hand), toxic (skull), oxidizing (flame over circle), irritant (exclamation), environmental hazard (dead fish/tree). Reading a bottle's labels before use is rule zero — the label tells you the PPE and spill response.

Fire triangle: fuel + oxygen + heat — remove one and fire dies: small alcohol flame? Cover with damp cloth/fire blanket (suffocate); never water on oil or electrical fires (spreads/energizes). A spilled acid? Neutralize with sodium hydrogen carbonate powder as directed, then wash.

Finally, the ethics and humility of the method: record raw data exactly as read (no 'tidying' to fit expectations — that's fraud, e.g. the cold-fusion scandal), report uncertainty, and accept that a rejected hypothesis is progress: it removes a wrong road for everyone. Chemistry's great discoveries (polythene, Teflon, penicillin's biology) came from careful observation of 'failed' experiments.

keyTerms.def: Gently fanning vapour toward the nose
Chemical that destroys living tissue/metals (acids, strong bases)
Others getting your result from your method

workedExamples.problem: Design a test for: 'sugar dissolves faster in hot water.' List IV, DV, two constants, the control.
workedExamples.answer: IV: water temperature; DV: dissolving time; constants: volume, mass of sugar, stirring rate; control: same setup at room temperature as baseline

workedExamples.problem: Why must you add acid to water rather than the reverse?
workedExamples.answer: Dilution is intensely exothermic; a drop of water entering concentrated acid flashes to steam and ejects acid droplets — pouring acid into a large water volume disperses the heat safely

workedExamples.problem: A group runs one trial, gets a perfect trend, and stops. What method step did they skip and why does it matter?
workedExamples.answer: Replication — one trial can't separate pattern from random error; conclusions need averaged repeats to be trusted

commonMistakes: Saying a hypothesis is 'proved' — evidence supports or fails to support
Testing two variables at once and not knowing which caused what
Tweaking numbers to match the expected answer (fraud, not fixing)
Pouring water into concentrated acid 'to dilute it'
applications: School practical exams (NCDC) test exactly these procedures — safety and fair tests score marks
Consumer skepticism: a supplement 'study' with no control or replication is marketing
Kitchen science: testing ripening/brewing conditions is hands-on method practice
Occupational: lab technicians, quality officers, health workers all apply the method daily
Climate/agriculture: farmers' field trials (one seed variety vs the usual plot = control) mirror this design
g9-chemistry-uc2-t2.summary: The method loops observation → hypothesis → controlled experiment (one variable, baseline, replicates) → analysis → conclusion → communication, with reproducibility as the gold standard. Safety is inseparable: PPE, wafting, acid-into-water, aware exits and fire-blanket response, hazard-symbol literacy. Honest data, even when it kills your hypothesis, is the whole point.
